records.title: Present simple and regular past
records.rule: Use the present simple for habits and facts (I walk to school), and add -ed for most past actions (Yesterday I walked).
records.examples: Every day she plays cricket. | Last week we visited Amma.
records.tip: Time words help: every day → present; yesterday, last week → past.
records.check_question: Choose the right verb: Yesterday we ___ to the park.
records.check_options: A. walk | B. walked | C. walks
records.check_explanation: Yesterday tells you it is the past: walked.
records.evidence_status: teaching content; status candidate: written by OpenPath for the first web version; not yet reviewed by educators; educator review: none

records.title: Common irregular past forms
records.rule: Many common verbs do not take -ed in the past: go → went, buy → bought, see → saw, eat → ate.
records.examples: We went to the market and bought mangoes. | I saw a film and ate popcorn.
records.tip: Learn these by heart; never write goed or buyed.
records.check_question: Choose the right verb: She ___ a new bag last week.
records.check_options: A. buyed | B. bought | C. buy
records.evidence_status: teaching content; status candidate: written by OpenPath for the first web version; not yet reviewed by educators; educator review: none

records.title: Questions and negatives with did
records.rule: After did and didn't, use the base form of the verb: Did you go? I didn't see it. (Not: Did you went?)
records.examples: Did she finish her homework? | We didn't watch TV.
records.tip: did already shows the past, so the verb stays in its base form.
records.check_options: A. saw | B. see | C. seen
records.check_explanation: After did, use the base form: see.
records.evidence_status: teaching content; status candidate: written by OpenPath for the first web version; not yet reviewed by educators; educator review: none

records.title: Keeping the tense steady
records.rule: When you tell a story in the past, keep it in the past: She opened the door and saw a dog. Learn less common irregular forms: catch → caught, choose → chose, lead → led.
records.examples: He caught the ball and threw it back. | They chose a leader who led them well.
records.tip: Read your sentences again and check every verb is in the same time.
records.check_question: Choose: The team ___ the cup last year.
records.check_options: A. win | B. won | C. wins
records.check_explanation: last year is the past: won.

records.title: Uncommon irregular forms
records.rule: Some irregular verbs are rare but appear in books: seek → sought, weep → wept, forbid → forbade, bear → bore.
records.examples: They sought help from the teacher. | She wept with joy.
records.tip: If you are unsure, check a dictionary: it lists irregular past forms.
records.check_question: Choose: The king ___ anyone to enter.
records.check_options: A. forbidded | B. forbade | C. forbid
records.evidence_status: teaching content; status candidate: written by OpenPath for the first web version; not yet reviewed by educators; educator review: none

records.title: He, she, it + -s
records.rule: In the present simple, add -s or -es to the verb after he, she, it or one person or thing: she sings, he fixes, the dog barks.
records.examples: My aunt teaches music. | It rains a lot in July.
records.tip: I, you, we, they: no -s (they play).
records.check_question: Choose: She ___ to music every evening.

records.title: Plural subjects
records.rule: A plural subject takes a plural verb: the mice run, the trees grow, my cousins live nearby.
records.examples: The birds are on the roof. | These shoes look new.
records.tip: Find the subject first, then match the verb to it.

records.title: Two subjects with and
records.rule: Two subjects joined by and take a plural verb: Anil and Sara are friends.
records.examples: My sister and I walk to school. | Bread and butter is…
records.tip: and adds the subjects together, so the verb is plural.
records.check_question: Choose: Tom and his dog ___ in the park.
records.check_explanation: Tom and his dog = two: are.

records.title: Words between subject and verb
records.rule: The verb agrees with the subject, not with a noun just before it: The jar of sweets is empty. The cup of tea is hot.
records.examples: The colour of the flowers is bright. | The boys in the team are tired.
records.tip: Cover the words between: 'The box … is'.
records.check_question: Choose: The basket of eggs ___ full.
records.check_explanation: The subject is the basket (one): is.

records.title: Each, every, everyone
records.rule: each, every, everyone, nobody and somebody take a singular verb: Each of the girls has a ticket. Everyone is here.
records.examples: Every child needs sleep. | Somebody is at the door.
records.tip: Each of the… is still one at a time: singular.
records.check_question: Choose: Each of the players ___ a shirt.

records.title: either … or, neither … nor
records.rule: With either … or and neither … nor, the verb agrees with the nearer subject: Neither the driver nor the passengers were hurt. Either the girls or their father is coming.
records.examples: Either my parents or my aunt is coming. | Neither the dog nor the cats were hungry.
records.tip: Look at the subject closest to the verb.
records.check_question: Choose: Neither Priya nor her brothers ___ at home.
records.check_explanation: The nearer subject, brothers, is plural: are.

records.title: Inverted order; a number of
records.rule: When the verb comes first, find the subject after it: There are many birds. Here comes the bus. 'A number of' is plural; 'the number of' is singular.
records.examples: A number of shops were closed. | The number of cars is growing.
records.tip: Turn the sentence round: many birds are there.
records.check_question: Choose: There ___ three books on the desk.
records.check_explanation: The subject is three books: are.

records.title: a or an
records.rule: Use an before a word that starts with a vowel (a, e, i, o, u) and a before a consonant: an orange, an egg, a ball, a cat.
records.examples: an inkpot, an onion | a pencil, a dog
records.tip: Say it aloud: 'an apple' is easier to say than 'a apple'.

records.title: a first, then the
records.rule: Use a when you first mention something, then the when you mention it again: I found a shell. The shell was pink. Use a before a job: He is a farmer.
records.examples: We bought a kite. The kite was red. | My uncle is a doctor.

records.title: a or an by sound
records.rule: Choose a or an by the first sound, not the first letter: an honour (silent h), an MP; a unicorn, a one-rupee coin (they start with 'yoo' and 'w' sounds).

records.title: the for one of a kind
records.rule: Use the for things there is only one of, or that everyone knows: the moon, the sky, the Prime Minister.
records.examples: The sky is clear today. | Close the door, please.
records.tip: If there is only one, it is the.

records.title: No a with uncountable nouns
records.rule: Some nouns cannot be counted: luggage, bread, water, news, rice. Do not use a or an with them: some luggage, a piece of bread.
records.examples: We bought some bread. | There is a lot of traffic today.

records.title: General statements
records.rule: For general statements about all of something, use no article with plurals and abstract nouns: Elephants are strong. Kindness is important.

records.title: Articles with names
records.rule: Most names of people, cities and countries have no article (Delhi, India), but rivers, oceans and some countries do: the Yamuna, the Indian Ocean, the United States. Mountains do not: Mount Abu.
